title: Facile synthesis of porous Cu-Sn alloy electrode with prior selectivity of formate in a wide potential range for CO2 electrochemical reduction
abstract: CO2 electroreduction is regarded as a potential way to mitigate CO2 level and produce value-added chemicals. Although Cu-Sn bimetallic electrodes show an excellent selectivity towards targeted formate or CO, the better performance is only achieved in a narrow potential range. Herein, porous Cu6.26Sn5 electrode is prepared. Alloying Cu with Sn atoms tunes the electronic structure of catalyst, which balances the adsorption and protonation of CO2* intermediate. The unique rice spike-like microstructure intensifies the local electric field to raise the CO2 concentration at the reaction sites. As a result, it exhibits a superior selectivity towards formate with the maximum faradaic efficiency (FEformate) of 97.8 ± 2.4 %. The better selectivity (FEformate over 80 %) is maintained over a wider potential range of 600 mV, which outperforms the majority of reported Cu-Sn bimetallic electrodes. This research provides a promising way to concurrently regulate morphological and electronic structure of alloy electrodes for efficient CO2 electroreduction.

Facile synthesis of porous Cu-Sn alloy electrode with prior selectivity of formate in a wide potential range for CO2 electrochemical reduction
Da Li a,b,1, Linlin Huang a,1, Yan Tian a, Tongtong Liu a, Liang Zhen b, Yujie Feng a,* a State Key Laboratory of Urban Water Resource and Environment, Harbin Institute of Technology, No 73 Huanghe Road, Harbin, Heilongjiang, 150090, China b School of Materials Science and Engineering, Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), Pingshan Road, Shen Zhen, Guangdong, 518055, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: CO2 electroreduction Porous Cu-Sn alloy electrode Formate Electric field intensity
A B S T R A C T
CO2 electroreduction is regarded as a potential way to mitigate CO2 level and produce value-added chemicals. Although Cu-Sn bimetallic electrodes show an excellent selectivity towards targeted formate or CO, the better performance is only achieved in a narrow potential range. Herein, porous Cu6.26Sn5 electrode is prepared. Alloying Cu with Sn atoms tunes the electronic structure of catalyst, which balances the adsorption and protonation of CO2*– intermediate. The unique rice spike-like microstructure intensifies the local electric field to raise the CO2 concentration at the reaction sites. As a result, it exhibits a superior selectivity towards formate with the maximum faradaic efficiency (FEformate) of 97.8 ± 2.4 %. The better selectivity (FEformate over 80 %) is maintained over a wider potential range of 600 mV, which outperforms the majority of reported Cu-Sn bimetallic electrodes. This research provides a promising way to concurrently regulate morphological and electronic structure of alloy electrodes for efficient CO2 electroreduction.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 into value-added chemicals and fuels has caused a great attention with respect to the advantages of decreasing CO2 concentration in atmosphere and providing “green” approach for energy sustainability [1–3]. Among all the possible products, formate (HCOO− ) or formic acid (HCOOH) as an attractive product is highly desirable because of its broad application in fuel cells, syngas conversion, and other industrial feedstock [4–6]. However, this process usually requires a high energy to activate the CO2 molecule due to its thermodynamically stable property. Generally, the formation of CO2
• – is regarded to be the rate-determining step of the CO2 electroreduction because the standard potential of CO2/CO2
• – couple reaches –1.9 V vs standard hydrogen electrode [7]. Therefore, robust catalysts are necessary to motivate this process. Copper has attracted great attention due to its capability for a variety of hydrocarbon and/or oxygenates productions [1,8–11]. However, the poor activity and selectivity are still far from satisfactory, which has hampered it from being commercialization.
Bimetallic electrocatalysts by introducing a secondary metal into Cu have exhibited an exciting performance in tunning the selectivity toward CO2 reduction. Based on Nørskov’s theoretical guidance,
developing bimetallic Cu-based catalysts can break the scaling relationship and lower the reaction overpotential by stabilizing the reaction intermediate [12]. The better catalytic performance of alloying two metals together over their monometallic counterparts is mainly attributed to the tuned electronic structure and geometric effects which change the binding strength of intermediates like CO2
• – [13,14]. To date, various Cu-based bimetallic catalysts such as Cu-Au [15–17], Cu-Pd [18–21], Cu-Ag [22–25], Cu-Pt [26–28] and Cu-Co [29] have been synthesized with an outstanding selectivity for CO or hydrocarbons. It is demonstrated that the selectivity of Cu-based bimetallic catalysts is dominated by the nature of the second metal in the CO2 electroreduction process [30]. Among all the metal catalysts, Sn shows an intrinsic selectivity towards formate but suffers from higher overpotential and poor stability at the same time [31]. Therefore, preparing Cu-Sn bimetallic catalyst is expected not only to improve the formate selectivity of Cu-based catalysts, but also decrease the overpotential and sustain a more stable activity compared to Sn-based catalysts. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation indicates that alloying Cu and Sn can suppress hydrogen and CO generation, thereby promoting formate selectivity [32]. Recently, Cu-Sn bimetallic electrocatalysts with core–shell structures [33,34], alloying structures [35,36], and heterostructures [37–40]

have been fundamentally investigated to demonstrate how the catalysts composition, shape and size, as well as phase and structure affect the electrochemical performance in terms of formate selectivity, faradaic efficiency and overpotential, etc. However, it is worthy to point out that most of these catalysts suffer from the impaired selectivity for formate especially at higher overpotentials, making it only excellent in a narrow voltage window. For example, the faradaic efficiency of formate (FEformate) obtained by the CuSn catalyst declines from maximum 86 % to only ~65 % when poised potential declines from − 1.04 to − 1.2 V vs. RHE (reverse hydrogen electrode), whereas faradaic efficiency of H2 (FEH2) increases by ~2 times. Even after incorporation of CuSn with rGO, FEformate drops below 50 % [36]. Similarly, the FEformate obtained by the CuSn nanowires declines by ~20 % with decreasing potential from − 1.0 to − 1.2 V vs. RHE, while FEH2 increases by 2.5 times [38]. Similar decrements are also reported with heterostructured CuSn, CuSn alloy and Cu@Sn, etc [34,35,37,40–42]. Such a drawback has not been caused much attention. After such massive research efforts, it is still of great challenge to explore the robust Cu-Sn catalysts for higher selectivity in a wide potential range. Considering the favored *OCHO pathway for formate production with a higher Sn content in the alloy, increasing Sn:Cu ratio in Cu-Sn alloy is highly appreciated. Meanwhile, the efficiency of CO2 electroreduction is closely dependent on CO2 concentration at higher overpotentials especially the inner space of the cathode [43]. Keeping this in mind, we prepare a serious of self-supported three-dimensional Cu-Sn alloy electrodes with higher Sn content. The optimized Cu6.26Sn5 electrode exhibits a higher activity and selectivity towards formate, achieving the maximum FEformate of 97.8 ± 2.4 % at –1.08 V vs. RHE and maintaining FEformate over 80 % in a wide potential range from –0.78 V to –1.38 V vs. RHE. The excellent performance is attributed to that the porous structure of electrode facilitates the mass transfer and the unique nanostructure enhances the local CO2 concentration around reaction interfaces. In addition, the interaction between Cu and Sn alters the electronic structure to tune the binding strength of intermediate CO2 • – which benefits to its protonation.

sections.heading: 2.1. Fabrication of porous Cu-Sn alloy electrodes
sections.text: Cu-Sn alloy electrodes were synthesized through hydrogen bubble templates method [44]. Before electrochemical deposition, high purity copper foils (≥ 99.95 %) with geometric area of 1 cm2 were cleaned with acetone, ethylene glycol, absolute ethyl alcohol and 1 M hydrochloric acid, consecutively. Finally, these pretreated copper foils were cleaned with distill water for electrochemical deposition. In a typical process, electrolyte was prepared with 0.2 M CuSO4 and 0.15 M SnSO4 in 1.5 M H2SO4 solution. Electrodeposition was conducted in a two-electrodes system with a pretreated Cu foil cathode and a platinum sheet anode at the distance of 2 cm. To investigate the effect of the electrodeposition current density and time on the morphological and electrochemical performance, various current density (1–4 A cm–2) and deposition time (10− 40 s) were employed using a DC potentiostat. After electrodeposition, all prepared electrodes were rinsed with distilled water thoroughly and then dried in a vacuum oven at 35℃ overnight before fixing into electrolysis cell. The Cu foam and Sn electrodes were also prepared similarly at current density of 4 A cm–2 for 20 s.

sections.heading: 2.2. Morphological and structural characterization
sections.text:
The morphology of the porous electrodes was investigated with scanning electron microscope (SEM, S-4700, Hitachi Ltd.) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, H-7650, Hitachi Ltd.). High resolution TEM (HR-TEM, FEI Talos F200×) was also used and high angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADFSTEM) in combination with energy disperse spectroscopy (EDS) were conducted at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD)
patterns of all samples were recorded using a Germany D8 ADVANCE Xray diffractometer (λ=0.154 nm) using Cu Kα source (60 kV and 80 mA), the 2θ ranged from 10◦ to 90◦. The element valence of foam electrodes was measured using the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) with a monochromatic Al Kα radiation at 1486.6 eV (XPS, PH1− 5700 ESCA system, US). The binding energies were calibrated using the adventitious C 1s spectra at 284.8 eV. Because the metallic state of Cu and Cu(I) had statistically similar binding energy values, Auger Cu LMM spectra were performed to further determine the Cu species.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical activities
sections.text:
Electrochemical activities were performed in a typical H-type cell separated by a Nafion 117 proton exchange membrane. The prepared electrodes as working electrode and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode (saturated KCl, +197 mV vs. standard hydrogen electrode) were placed in one chamber, and a platinum sheet (1 cm2) as counter electrode was fixed in another chamber. The electrolyte used in both chambers was 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution, but the catholyte was bubbled with pure N2 or CO2 for at least 30 min before the tests. The Linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) was operated from –0.2 to –1.2 V vs. RHE at 10 mV s–1 in both N2 and CO2-saturated electrolyte. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed at –1.07 V with the frequency range from 100 kHz to 10 mHz at amplitude of 10 mV. The results were fitted with equivalent circuit to evaluate the charge transfer resistance during CO2 reduction. Adsorption affinity of hydroxyl was measured by oxidized LSV scan from – 0.4 to 0.6 V at 10 mV s–1 in N2-bubbled 0.1 M KOH electrolyte. All potentials were tested against Ag/AgCl reference electrode and then converted into RHE according to the following Equation
E (vs. RHE) = E (vs.Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 V + 0.0591 V × pH (1)

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical reduction of CO2
sections.text:
The CO2 reduction was also performed using the H-type cell with controlled potential by a potentiostat (WonATech WMPG 1000, Korea) under ambient pressure at room temperature. Prior to reduction, the electrolyte was purged with CO2 to remove air for at least 30 min and controlled at ~10 mL min–1 during the CO2 reduction. At the end of the reaction, gas products were detected using a gas chromatography (GC, Agilent 7890B) and liquid mixture was identified by ion chromatography (IC 6100, Anhui Wayeal) equipped with Dionex Ionpac™ AS11− HC separation column. The Faradaic efficiency of any products are calculated as following:
FE = αnF Q × 100% (2)
Where α is the mole of formate, n is the number of electrons transferred from CO2 to certain product, F is Faraday constant of 96,485 C mol–1, Q is the total charge passed across the cathodic electrode during the electrolysis (C).
The energy efficiency (EE) is defined the overall energy utilization toward the formate in this study, and calculated as equation below [45]:
EE = Eeq
Eeq + η FE (3)
Where Eeq is the equilibrium potential for formate, η and FE are the overpotential and the faraday efficiency of formate at certain potentials.

sections.heading: 2.5. Electric field simulation and calculation
sections.text:
The distribution of electric field intensity on the prepared porous Cu, Sn, and alloy electrodes were simulated with the COMSOL Multiphysics. The nanostructures of these three electrodes have been simplified based
D. Li et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 292 (2021) 120119
on the SEM images, and variations of the electric field densities with different applied potentials were simulated.
The turn over frequency (TOF, s–1) of Cu, Sn, and alloy electrodes for CO2-to-formate conversion is calculated at different applied potentials according to the Equation [46]:
TOF = i0 × FE
active site density × e × n (4)
where i0 (A cm− 2) is the current density at poised potential, FEformate is the faradaic efficiency of formate, e is the elementary charge (1.602 × 10–19 C) and n refers to the number of electrons transferred to generate formate (n = 2). For the active site density, the assumption was all active sites were electrochemically accessible. The active site density can be roughly calculated by XPS results and the mass loading on the working electrode.

sections.heading: 3.1. Preparation and morphology characterization of the alloy electrode
sections.text:
Porous Cu-Sn alloy electrodes are electrodeposited on Cu foil by dynamic hydrogen template-assisted method (Scheme 1). In this process, hydrogen bubbles are continuously formed at controlled current density, and serve as geometric template for ionic reduction at the spaces of the substrate where no hydrogen evolution occurs. To tune the morphology and structure of electrodes, electrodeposition is controlled at various current densities (1–4 A cm–2) with different deposition times (10− 40 s) as shown in Fig. 1. It is observed that porous structure is easily formed when current density reaches higher than 1 A cm–2. Pore size of the electrodes increases obviously with deposition time at identical current density at the sacrifice of pore number, this is because the hydrogen bubbles coalesces gradually during the deposition process. As expectation, the structure of pore-walls closely depends on the applied current density. Specifically, the wall is initially composed of small grains and gradually transform into grain-dendrite mixture when increases current density from 1 to 3 A cm–2, and finally the wall is mainly built of small dendrites at 4 A cm–2. Such an evolution tendency towards dendritic structures can be attributed to the transport limitation of ions [22]. At higher current densities, the reduction rate of ions near the Cu foil goes faster than their diffusion rate so that mass transportation becomes the dominant factor in tailoring the crystal shape. Without enough supply of ions, thermodynamically unstable dendritic nanostructures are predominantly formed.
With identical method, porous Cu and Sn electrodes are also prepared at 4 A cm− 2 for 20 s. From Fig. S1, quite different structures are observed from both electrodes. The Cu electrode is characterized by the maize-like secondary structure, which is similar to the reported mesoporous Cu foam, although deposited at lower current density [47]. By comparison, pine needle-shaped tin branches are intricately intertwined
to form gauze-like slimsy Sn framework [31]. The average pore diameter of outermost surface of Sn was ~150 μm, 4.3 times large than that of porous Cu electrode.
The morphological, compositional and structural analyses of the alloy electrodes prepared at 4 A cm–2 for 20 s are further characterized by combing SEM, HR-TEM, and HAADF-STEM inspection. From the top view image in Fig. 2a, it is clearly showed the pore diameter at the surface layer of the electrode ranges from 60 to 160 μm. Actually, there is a certain gradient in pore diameter from the surface of the Cu substrate upwards the top layer of electrode due to the gradual coalescence of H2 bubbles. These interconnected pores are expected to efficiently convey CO2, electrolyte, and the products in and out of the catalyst layer. Taking a close observation of the alloy electrode, the framework is constructed by massive dendritic rice spike-like secondary structures which stretches randomly into various directions (Fig. 2b-d). Based on the previous research, such an unique structure can provide a higher surface area of electrode [22]. HR-TEM image (Fig. 2e) clearly reveals the polycrystalline structure of electrode. From the selected alloy dendrite, lattice fringe distances are measured to be 0.210 and 0.296 nm, corresponding to the crystal plane (110) and (101) of Cu6.26Sn5, indicating the successful preparation of Cu-Sn alloy which will be further confirmed by XRD results. HAADF-STEM imaging and EDS analysis (Fig. 2f–i) confirm a uniform distribution of Cu and Sn throughout the selected bulk region of dendrite.

sections.heading: 3.2. Crystal structure and atomic composition of the electrode
sections.text:
Among all the electrodes prepared at different electrodeposition times, the samples obtained at 20 s for alloy is chosen to analyze the bulk crystalline structure. As noted in the X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern in Fig. 3a, all reflection peaks correspond to the hexagonal Cu6.26Sn5 [JCPDS No. 47-1575] except the metallic Cu peaks at 2θ = 50.54◦ due to the exposure of Cu substrate. No other impurities are observed which confirms the high crystallinity of Cu6.26Sn5. The atomic ratio in the alloy electrode confirmed by the XRD result is well consistent with the mole ratio of ionic concentration (nCu2+: nSn2+ = 1.3) in the precursor solution. The XRD pattern of Cu foam electrode indicates the polycrystalline face-centered cubic Cu [JCPDS cards No. 04-0836] with (111), (200), and (220) diffraction peaks at 43.30◦, 50.43◦, and 74.13◦. Despite of the identical diffraction peaks with those of Cu foil, the remarkable deviation of I200:I111 = 0.40 and I220:I111 = 0.67 reflect the dominating (111) facet or the preferential orientation along (111) direction [47]. In addition, a weak peak at 36.42◦ can be indexed to the (111) planes of Cu2O which is attributed to the inevitable oxidation of Cu surface. The oxidation situation is also detected on porous Sn electrode as peaks at 27.48◦ belongs to (110) plane of SnO2, other reflection peaks are assigned to the body-centered tetragonal β-Sn phase [48].
XPS analysis is carried out to detect the surface composition of the prepared porous electrodes (Figure S2). From the high-resolution XPS in Fig. 3b, it is noted that the Cu 2p spectra of the new prepared Cu and

Cu6.26Sn5 show two typical peaks at 932.4 eV (Cu 2p3/2) and 952.2 eV (Cu 2p1/2), which belong to the Cu (0) and/or Cu (I). The Auger spectra further demonstrates only Cu (0) presents in the pure Cu and Cu6.26Sn5
electrodes as the peak locates around 567.8 eV (Figure S3). Although the same chemical states in Cu and Cu6.26Sn5 electrodes, a slightly negative shift in the Cu 2p3/2 is observed from Cu6.26Sn5, indicating the charge
D. Li et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 292 (2021) 120119
redistribution after alloying Sn. Comparing the Cu 2p spectra of Cu6.26Sn5 electrodes before and after CO2 reduction, there are no changes regarding to the Cu chemical states, indicating the metallic Cu is maintained well during the reduction process. This metallic state atoms can afford more electrochemical activated sites for CO2 hydrogenation [43].
In the Sn 3d spectra (Fig. 3c), both Sn and Cu6.26Sn5 (before and after CO2 reduction) show the SnOx at about 486.8 (3d5/2) and 495.3 eV (3d3/2) and small shoulder peaks at 485.1 (3d5/2) and 493.7 eV (3d3/2) assign to the Sn (0), indicating a higher content of SnOx at the surface layer of all samples. The content of Sn (0) in Cu6.26Sn5 is calculated to be double times higher than that of its metallic counterpart, but declines slightly after CO2 reduction (Figure S4). Learning that Sn oxidation is highly spontaneous occurred when exposed to air, it is deduced that the generated Sn (0) have been partially oxidized again, leading to the lower content of Sn (0) after CO2 reduction. In contrast to Cu 2p, the Sn 3d peaks of the Cu6.26Sn5 electrode slightly shifts to a higher binding energy (0.2 eV), again suggesting the electron transfer from Sn to Cu atoms [49]. Based on the above analyses, the Cu6.26Sn5 electrodes are yielded with surface components dominated by Cu and Sn after CO2 reduction [50].

sections.heading: 3.3. Electrochemical CO2 reduction
sections.text:
Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements of alloy electrodes prepared at different deposition times (10− 40 s at 4 A cm–2) and current densities (1–5 A cm–2 for 20 s) are carried out from 0.2 to –1.2 V vs RHE in CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 solution at a scan rate of 10 mV s–1 as showed in Figure S5. It can be notified that Cu-Sn alloy electrode prepared at 4 A cm–2 for 20 s exhibits the highest current density among all the prepared electrodes. Compared to this condition, shortening deposition time (10 s) or decreasing deposition current density (1–3 A cm–2) achieved thinner metallic porous framework which impairs the CO2 reduction activity as a result of less reaction sites. Whereas prolonging time (30− 40 s) or applying higher current density (5 A cm–2) yields thicker catalyst layers so that the surface layer will be easily oxidized. Meanwhile, the enlarged pore diameter and therefore smaller pore density possibly reduce the electroactive surface area [31]. All these account for how the electrochemical activity varies with the morphological and structural features.
LSV curves between Cu6.26Sn5 and its monometallic electrodes are further compared to evaluate their electrochemical performance towards CO2 reduction. As shown in Fig. 4a, porous Cu and Cu6.26Sn5 electrodes exhibit the similar current densities when the potentials are positive than –0.8 V, whereas remarkably higher current density is achieved with Cu6.26Sn5 electrode with increased overpotentials. As for the Sn electrodes (Fig. 4a and S6), the obvious reduction peaks ranged from –0.20 ~ –0.45 V are attributed to the reduction of tin oxide formed easily when they are exposed to air [51]. More intriguingly, both Cu and Sn electrodes have a relatively lower onset potential which starts about –0.5 and –0.7 V, respectively. In comparison, the onset potential of Cu6.26Sn5 shifts positively to about –0.4 V. The dramatical enhancement of catalytic activity of Cu6.26Sn5 indicates the synergic effect after alloying Cu and Sn into one electrode [52]. When compares current density in N2- and CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (Fig. 4b and Figure S6), the higher current density generated in CO2 reveals the participation of CO2 electroreduction because the reduction product like formate and CO are detected.
The faradaic efficiency for different products obtained at different potentials are compared to evaluate the selectivity of each electrode (Fig. 4c–e). As for the porous Sn electrodes, when the potential is controlled negatively from –0.38 to –1.38 V vs RHE, formate starts to be produced at –0.78 V and the faradaic efficiency of formate (FEformate) increases gradually and approaches the maximum of 80.7 ± 1.6 % at –1.18 V. Compared to formate, CO is detectable at –0.58 V while the maximum FECO is only 20.3 ± 4.9 % achieved at –0.68 V, and then it decreases slightly at larger overpotentials possibly due to the higher formate selectivity. As the competing reaction, H2 production presents the opposite trend to formate. Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) dominates the electrode reaction at lower overpotential but it drops to the minimum where FEformate is obtained and then slightly increases up to 20 %.
With regarding to porous Cu electrodes, H2 is the dominant product when the applied potential is controlled positive than –0.58 V. Increasing the overpotential efficiently facilitates CO2 reduction by restraining the HER. Therefore, FEformate gradually increases, reaching the maximum of 44.5 ± 2.1 % at –1.18 V (Fig. 4d). Similar to the Sn electrode, favoring formate production results in the lower FECO. It has been proposed that the transfer of proton–electron to the adsorbed CO2 would generate *COOH and *OCHO which have been considered to be
D. Li et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 292 (2021) 120119
the key intermediates for CO and formate formation [53]. Therefore, the favorable selectivity towards formate would possibly impair the parallel CO pathway. More importantly, hydrocarbon like C2H4 and CH4 have been produced at potentials –0.68 and –0.88 V, respectively. It is easy to find the FEC2H4 and FECH4 show a converse trend to FECO. A similar variation of CO production against other products is also detected with AgCu foam electrode, demonstrating the C2 products are produced from CO intermediates [54].
After alloying Cu and Sn together, the formate, CO and H2 as the dominated products are yielded with Cu6.26Sn5 (Fig. 4e). Compared to the products selectivity of Cu, Cu6.26Sn5 efficiently impedes the production of multi-electrons products like CH4 and C2H4. This is consistent with previous report which indicates that one of the reasons for the diminished hydrocarbon production is possibly attributed to the protonation of CO* due to the lower surface coverage of H* [55]. Although Cu6.26Sn5 electrode shows the same selectivity to Sn electrode, it presents much higher activity for CO2 reduction in terms of lower overpotential and higher faradaic efficiency towards formate. Specifically, the onset potential for format shifts with 400 mV positive to –0.38 V after alloying Cu with Sn. In addition, the FEformate reaches the maximum of 97.8 ± 2.4 % at –1.08 V, which increases by 21.3 % compared to that of porous Sn (80.6 ± 1.6 %) at –1.18 V. Although some Cu-Sn electrodes
(Figure S7) and other bimetallic electrodes (Table S1) achieve the maximum FEformate at very close potential, the selectivity for formate with Cu6.26Sn5 in this study is higher than the majority reports. For example, maximum FEformate at –1.08 V in this report is almost 2.4 times higher than that of Cu3Sn at –1.09 V [55]. More significantly, FEH2 is restrained blow 10 % in a wide range of –0.78 ~ –1.38 V on Cu6.26Sn5. Previous reports always depict that the HER is boosted over CO2 reduction on electrode as the limitation of CO2 transport at higher overpotentials decreases the CO2 concentration in the aqueous electrolyte [46,56]. However, the inter-connective porous structure of Cu6.26Sn5 affords plenty of pore channels to substantially impel CO2 diffusion to reaction sites, thereby maintaining the prosperous CO2 reduction. It has also been demonstrated that the suppression of the HER on Cu3Sn(002) is derived from the decrease in the number of reaction sites for H2 evolution after alloying Cu with Sn which weakens the adsorption of H* [55]. From Fig. 4f, we compare the potential dependance of FEformate of Cu6.26Sn5 with that of state-of-art Cu-Sn based bimetallic electrodes. It is obviously noticed that the prepared Cu6.26Sn5 in this study outperforms the majority of reported CuSn alloy electrodes especially when cathode potential lowers than –1.0 V where the FEformate of Cu6.26Sn5 can still be maintained over 80 %.
Energy efficiency (EE) is calculated further based on the performance
D. Li et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 292 (2021) 120119
of CO2-to-formate production at different potentials (Figure S8). Compared to the consistently dropping trend of EE by porous Cu, the EE obtained by Cu6.26Sn5 and Sn are enhanced with increased overpotential but maintains almost unchanged before the potential reaches over –1.18 V. The maximum EE is 39.5 %, 30.7 % and 20.0 % for Cu6.26Sn5, Sn, and Cu electrode, respectively. Overall, the opposite tendency between formate and hydrogen as well as the higher FEformate (＞80 %) in a wider potential range reveal the better catalytic performance of Cu6.26Sn5 toward CO2-to-formate conversion. The superior performance of Cu6.26Sn5 electrode than its monometallic counterparts towards CO2 electroreduction is possibly attributed to the intrinsic activity of the electroactive sites by alloying Cu with Sn [57].

sections.heading: 3.4. Mechanism analysis of alloy electrode for CO2 electroreduction
sections.text:
To gain an insight into the mechanistic pathway of CO2 reduction, Tafel plots of all three electrodes are compared and shown in Fig. 5a. As commonly acknowledges that CO2 electroreduction starts with an electron transfer to CO2 molecule to form CO2*–, then the protonation of adsorbed CO2*– triggers a second electron transfer to generate HCOO– as described below:
CO2 + e− →CO∗−2 (ads) (1)
CO∗−2 (ads) + H +→OCHO(ads) (2)
OCHO(ads) + e− →HCO−2(ads) (3)
As shown in Fig. 5a, the Tafel slope of Sn and Cu electrodes are 325 and 312 mV dec–1, respectively. Whereas it decreases to only 136 mV dec–1 for Cu6.26Sn5. The declined Tafel slope implies alloying Cu and Sn together can boost the reaction kinetics for the CO2-to-formate conversion. In addition, the value close to 120 mV dec–1 demonstrates that the first electron transfer to form the intermediate CO2*– is identified to be the rate-determining step. To explore the electro-transfer activity during CO2 electroreduction, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is carried out at a constant potential of –1.08 V (Fig. 5b). Fitting with the equivalent circuit, the ohmic resistance (Rohm) for all electrodes is
similar with an average of 15.4 ± 0.4 Ω, while charge transfer resistance (Rct) declines remarkably after alloying Cu with Sn (9.5 Ω), which is only 50.5 % and 21.9 % of that obtained with Sn (18.8 Ω) and Cu (43.4 Ω) electrodes, indicating a faster charge transfer process between electrode and adsorbed CO2.
The kinetics of CO2 reduction will be controlled from charge transfer to mass diffusion process with increasing overpotential, maintaining sufficiently available CO2 is regarded to be an essential factor to achieve a prosperous performance of CO2 electroreduction [58], it is therefore deduced that the better electrochemical activity of porous Cu6.26Sn5 is closely attributed to the higher CO2 concentration at the microenvironment of reaction sites. Knowing from that the nanostructure of catalysts plays a crucial role in altering the local CO2 concentration by changing the interfacial electric field density (EFD) [59,60], the prepared Cu, Sn and Cu6.26Sn5 are clearly assembled by distinct secondary nanostructures, it is therefore anticipated that the distribution of EFD around these unique sites will be much different. We firstly evaluate the EFD distribution at cathodic potential of –1.08 V. Based on the COMSOL simulation result (Fig. 5c, d), it is easy to observe the great impact of nanostructure of catalyst on electric field intensity. Specifically, the EFD value obtained by Cu6.26Sn5 is 1.82 and 1.34 times higher than that of Cu and Sn electrodes. The intensive EFD of alloy electrode is mainly allocated around the spiky point as demonstrated with Au nanoneedles [59], Bi nanosheets [60], and Cu@Sn nanocones [34]. As a high-curvature structure, these spiky points can concentrate higher ions like K+ which will attract more CO2 moving towards these sites and further activate these CO2 based on the field-induced reagent concentration theory [59]. To further investigate the variation of EFD with the applied potentials, simulations at potential range of –0.38 ~ –1.38 V are carried out. In Fig. 5c and Figure S9, the linear increment of EFD with more negative potentials is obtained for all electrodes, among which Cu6.26Sn5 displays the highest value at the same potentials, and the difference becomes more distinct at larger overpotentials. Although the EFD simulation fails to estimate the CO2 concentration, it points out that higher CO2 concentration will be aroused even at more negative potential. To confirm this, the partial current density vs. applied potential is plotted. As depicted in Figure S10, the current density for formate (jformate) constantly increases, and there is no jformate limitation in the
D. Li et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 292 (2021) 120119
tested potential range. The higher CO2 concentration is not only related to the intensive EFD as a result of unique nanostructure, but also closely dependent on the porous cathode structure. It has been widely acknowledged that HER would be boosted on cathode especially in higher KHCO3 solutions at higher overpotentials because the ratio of dissolved CO2 (the real reactant) to the total carbonate declines as the KHCO3 concentrations [58]. In order to manifests the significance of porous structure on CO2 reduction performance, CO2 reduction is further carried out in CO2-saturated KHCO3 electrolyte with different concentrations (0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 M) at –1.38 V. From the FE and particle current density results (Figure S11), FEH2 only increases from 9.7 to 11.9% as KHCO3 concentrations increases from 0.1 to 0.5 M, whereas FEformate is still maintained over 80 % although it slightly declines from 87.3 % in 0.3 M KHCO3 to 80.8 % in 0.5 M KHCO3. Meanwhile, KHCO3 concentrations plays a positive effect on improving the jformate which is 1.4 and 2.4 times higher in 0.5 M KHCO3 compared to that in 0.3 and 0.1 M solution. This better activity implies the porous structure of Cu6.26Sn5 conveys more reactant CO2 to the reaction interfaces. This is supported by our previous study that the porous three-dimensional (3D) foam electrode lowers the mass transfer resistance by affording abundant pore channels at larger overpotentials [31]. It should be clarified that the EFD effects caused by K+ will be independent of its concentration [61,62], therefore, the better CO2 diffusion should be attributed to the integrative effects of interconnected pore channels of 3D structure and spiky feature.
It is known that the product selectivity closely depends on the binding energy of the adsorbed intermediates [63]. CO2*– radical as one of the key intermediates will be firstly generated during CO2 electroreduction. To determine how binding strength of CO2*– changes before and after alloying Cu and Sn together, hydroxyl is chosen as a surrogate of CO2*– to evaluate its adsorption energy on different catalysts by oxidative LSV scan in N2-saturated 0.1 M NaOH [64]. From Fig. 5e, the potential for oxidative adsorption of hydroxyl is more negative on Cu electrode and more positive on Sn electrode, indicating the strong and weak binding of OH–, respectively [65,66]. In the case of the Cu electrode, the high adsorption strength will increase the barrier of CO2*– to be further reduced (protonation), whereas the lower adsorption on Sn electrode implies more energy requirements for the formation of
intermediate, which causes larger overpotentials as Fig. 4c depicted [64]. In comparison, Cu6.26Sn5 has a moderate potential for binding OH–, demonstrating alloying Cu with Sn can effectively tune the binding strength of intermediate CO2*– possibly by altering the electronic structure of the catalyst [24]. In order to illustrate the change of electronic structure, the density of states (DOS) between Cu6.26Sn5 and Cu is compared. Figure S12 clearly indicates that the total DOS of Cu6.26Sn5 is formed by the main D-orbitals of Cu and slight p-orbitals of Sn, and the D-band center decreases from –2.84 eV for the Cu to –3.14 eV for the Cu6.26Sn5. Comparison of projected DOS (pDOS) also shows the D-band centers of Cu in the Cu6.26Sn5 is lower than those in pure Cu, all these illustrate the change of electronic structure after alloying Cu and Sn together. The decreased D-band center of alloy electrode will weaken the adsorption of intermediate on the reaction sites [67], which confirms the result of Fig. 5e. The moderate adjustment of the intermediate CO2*– binding balances the energy requirements for CO2 activation and the following CO2*– protonation, which can be another significant reason for the highly efficient CO2-to-formate conversion.
It is also worth to note from Fig. 4 c–e that Cu6.26Sn5 exhibits higher CO2-to-formate conversion at – 0.58 V with a Faradaic efficiency nearly 60 %, whereas Sn electrode dominantly produces H2 and Cu electrode shows lower selectivity towards both CO and formate. These results imply the alloying process efficiently improves the selectivity towards formate by depressing the HER and CO pathway. The intrinsic activities of three electrodes are then investigated by active surface area (ECSA)normalized partial current density of formate (jformate), CO (jCO) and hydrogen (jH2) at certain potentials. It is obviously observed from Fig. 6a that the jformate is consistently higher than that of Cu and Sn. Although jCO and jH2 varied irregularly among these electrodes (Fig. 6b, c), Cu6.26Sn5 always presents the lowest values compared to Cu and Sn electrode, manifesting the excellent selectivity towards formate is benefit from the suppressing HER and CO production efficiently. It is reported that increasing Sn content in Cu-Sn alloy will lead to the preferred selectivity from CO to formate because the composition change weakens the *COOH but strengthens the adsorption of *OCHO by changing the electronic structure [49]. Combining the XPS and DOS results, the rearrangement of electron structure of Cu6.26Sn5 favors the *OCHO pathway over *COOH, making formate as the main product.

Based on the above analyses, we propose a possible mechanism of CO2 reduction on Cu6.26Sn5 electrode: (i) most CO2 molecules are adsorbed on adjacent Cu-Sn binding sites in the form of Sn-O [49,68]; (ii) one electron transfers either from Cu or from Sn atom to the adsorbed CO2 to form CO2*–; (iii) the formed CO2*– is in the state in which the C atom is available for hydrogenation to generate HCOO*; (iv) after acquiring a secondary electron, the produced HCOO– is bound weakly on these sites and released into electrolyte as illustrated in Fig. 5f.
Turnover frequency (TOF) for formate formation is expected to be boosted as a result of the alteration of the binding strength on alloy electrode. As shown in Fig. 6d, the TOF of Cu6.26Sn5 is higher than those of Sn and much higher than that of Cu electrode in the potential range of –0.78 ~ –1.38 V. For example, the TOF of Cu6.26Sn5 is 1.2 and 2.1 times larger than that of Sn and Cu at the potential of –1.18 V, suggesting the efficient per-site activity of alloy electrode for formate production.

sections.heading: 3.5. Stability of porous electrodes for CO2 reduction
sections.text: Long-term stability of electrodes is also an important factor to estimate the performance for CO2 reduction. Therefore, the continuous electrochemical reduction is carried out for 10 h at –1.18 V (porous Cu and Sn) and –1.08 V (Cu6.26Sn5) where maximum faradaic efficiencies are obtained in CO2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte, and the products are analyzed every one hour. It is notable from Fig. 7a that the current densities of Cu6.26Sn5 remain constant at around 8.5 mA cm− 2 during 10 h with an average FEformate of 92.8 %. Although FEformate slightly declines from initial 96.0%–90.4% at the end of the test, the negligible deactivation signifies a superior stability of Cu6.26Sn5 electrode. This stable performance outperforms the porous Cu and Sn electrodes as the FEformate begins to drop from 51.2 % and 83.5 % to about 25.7 % and 75.2 % after electrolyzing for 1 h and keeps almost unchanged in the following hours. It is demonstrated that the morphology and structure of catalyst/cathode plays a key role in maintaining its stability [69,70]. SEM images of porous electrodes are thereby characterized after 10 h of electrochemical reaction. The distinct structure is observed with Sn electrodes where the porous structure totally collapses, leaving a rod (bottom)-branch (upper) overlapped structure (Figure S14). Intriguingly, the Cu6.26Sn5 electrode maintains the integrity of entire structure, showing little change in terms of pore diameter, the dendritic rice spike-like secondary structures, and the pore-walls, demonstrating the alloying Cu with Sn prevents the electrode from being deformed, which therefore benefits to sustain its stability. In view of the higher FEformate over a wide potential window, lower overpotential, faster reaction kinetics and excellent stability, the Cu6.26Sn5 is a promising candidate for CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we prepare a porous Cu-Sn alloy electrode by a simple and facile electrodeposition method. By optimizing the preparation condition, the structure of the porous Cu6.26Sn5 is tuned which has typical dendritic microstructure. Such a unique structure leads to a higher local electrical field which is beneficial to absorb more CO2 molecules around the reaction sites. The alloying Cu and Sn also tunes electronic structure to facilitate electron transfer and moderate the binding strength of intermediate CO2*–, thereby balances the activation energy of CO2 and the protonation of CO2*–. Cu6.26Sn5 exhibits an superior electrochemical reduction of CO2 to formate with the maximum FEformate of 97.8 ± 2.4 % as well as higher per-site activity. More importantly, it could maintain the FEformate over 80 % in a wider potential range (–0.78 ~ –1.38 V vs. RHE). This research can provide a new way for alloy electrodes to regulate surface and electronic structure concurrently toward efficient CO2-to-formate electroreduction.
